title: 1.1 Meet the People
unit_outcome: Understand and produce simple sentences about people, family members, and actions.
goal: Identify a boy, girl, man, and woman, then use he or she in a short identity sentence.
grammar_function: A + singular person; He/She is a + singular person.
prerequisite: No prior English is required; this is the first course lesson.
speaking_outcome: Say short identity phrases and connect a person noun to he or she.

cards.pedagogy_note: The first person arrives; a introduces one person with boy.
The opening boy remains visible while the noun changes to the pronoun he.
The first two anchors combine into the lesson's first complete sentence.
A second child joins the same meet-the-people sequence.
The opening girl remains visible while the learner connects her to the pronoun she.
The girl follows the same noun-to-pronoun-to-sentence pattern as the boy.
The story now introduces the adult male counterpart to the boy.
The adult male immediately receives the same he-is-a identity frame learned with the boy.
The fourth person completes the cast after the man.
The adult female immediately receives the matching she-is-a identity frame.
The learner first separates child from adult within the male pair.

cards.spanish_translation: Elige la frase para el niño.
cards.pedagogy_note: The boy story immediately grows from the noun to the complete sentence in a new format.
The matching female age contrast follows naturally.

cards.spanish_translation: Elige la frase para la niña.
cards.pedagogy_note: The girl now receives the same noun-to-sentence treatment as the boy.
All four people now appear together as distinct visual categories.
The known he-is-a frame grows from boy to man.

cards.spanish_translation: Elige la frase para el hombre.
cards.pedagogy_note: The man is retrieved from a fresh image before the story moves to the woman.
The four-person contrast returns at the final story character.
The matching she-is-a frame grows from girl to woman.

cards.spanish_translation: Elige la frase para la mujer.
cards.pedagogy_note: Recognition ends on the adult counterpart, ready for audio-only retrieval.
Audio removes the visible target text while preserving the first age contrast.
The complete boy sentence follows the noun while the choice set expands.
The female age contrast immediately mirrors the previous card.
The complete girl sentence mirrors the boy sequence in a four-image format.
The learner now retrieves the complete male identity sentence by ear.
The man is now recognized from audio among complete written sentences.
The complete female identity sentence follows in the same structure.
Listening closes by retrieving the woman sentence in a different response format.
Production begins with the shortest familiar boy phrase.
The boy story grows immediately from noun phrase to full sentence.
The learner expands from a noun phrase to the complete girl sentence.
The same frame transfers from the child to the adult man.

title: 1.13 ¡Todos a la celebración!
unit_outcome: Understand and produce simple sentences about people, family members, and actions.
goal: Bring every person to one family celebration by finding people, connecting relationships, following actions, correcting false clues, and answering who they are.
grammar_function: Apply every Unit 1 identity, article, singular/plural, pronoun, action, negative, and who-question pattern inside one continuous celebration adventure.
speaking_outcome: Answer all three who-question forms and identify the reunited family aloud across four consecutive voice challenges.

cards.audio_text: A boy. A girl. A man. A woman.
cards.pedagogy_note: Mission beat 01/24: the learner follows one English clue and discovers how the game responds; the completed interaction advances the same family celebration adventure.

audio_assets.text: La celebración está por comenzar y todavía faltan invitados. Escucha cada frase, encuentra a las personas y descubre qué están haciendo. Al final responderás en voz alta para abrir la celebración. Primero practicaremos juntos.

title: 3.1 Greetings and Names

title: 3.3 Am, Is, and Are
unit_outcome: Use tightly supported exchanges to greet people and give a name, age, origin and job, ask and answer yes/no questions with be, and describe who owns things.
goal: Ask what you, she, he and they are doing, and follow each question with an answer using a familiar action.
grammar_function: What are you doing? / I am ...; What is she doing? / She is ...; What is he doing? / He is ...; What are they doing? / They are ... . Complete present-progressive exchanges using familiar Unit 1 actions; do/does is not generalized.
prerequisite: 3.2 I/you/we frames plus Unit 1 he/she/they, is/are, actions, baby and babies.
speaking_outcome: Say all four current-action questions and their matching answers in separate consecutive turns.

prerequisite: 1.8 not; 3.2 I/you; 3.3 am/is/are and What are you doing?.

title: 3.16 Cenas cruzadas
unit_outcome: Meet people, exchange personal information established in dialogue, ask and answer yes/no questions, describe ownership, and ask about the current action.
goal: Help Ana run the community center's international dinner: recognize who says each greeting and introduction, meet the guests' countries, ages and jobs, follow what everyone is doing and owns, and answer five dinner-table questions aloud.
grammar_function: Hello/Good morning/Goodbye; What is your name? My name is...; I am/you are/we are; he/she is, they are; What are you doing? I am + -ing; I am ... years old; I am from... / I am + nationality; I am a + job; my/your/his/her + noun; have/has. These books are ours.; It is the woman's phone.; Is this phone yours? title: 4.10 What Time Is It?
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, describe a short daily routine, ask and answer Do you...? questions, and say the day and the time.
goal: Identify morning, afternoon, evening and night from contextual scenes, then ask and answer the time, read whole hours and distinguish a.m. from p.m.
grammar_function: It is morning/afternoon/evening/night; What time is it? It is + number + o'clock; in the morning / in the afternoon / in the evening / at night; It is + number + a.m./p.m. No routines or activity-at-time statements.
prerequisite: Units 2–3 numbers 1–12, it/is; 4.3 in/the; 4.5 in the morning. No routine verbs are required.
speaking_outcome: Name the part of the day, take both roles in a time exchange and give a clear whole-hour answer with its day period.

title: 6.1 Places Around Town
unit_outcome: Name places and transport, explain a current destination, complete a trip, follow directions, ask for help, choose a service and check its times.
goal: Name useful places, locate familiar people, and connect a place with a familiar need.
grammar_function: Ana and her family make a short neighborhood visit. Start at the station, locate the father at the bank and the mother at the pharmacy, find the children at the library, then meet at the mall and get food at the supermarket. Explicit Spanish transitions explain each change of location; the English stays within the early lesson’s scope.
prerequisite: Units 1–5 and the earlier Unit 6 lessons in the displayed course sequence.
speaking_outcome: Name useful places, locate familiar people, and connect a place with a familiar need.

title: 7.15 Un día con amigos
unit_title: Unit 7: Everyday Needs and A1 Integration
unit_outcome: Complete the grand multi-challenge A1 capstone synthesizing all units into one cohesive celebration event.
lesson_title: Unit 7: Everyday Needs and A1 Integration
goal: Prepare, travel, solve a misunderstanding and join friends at the park.
grammar_function: Apply previously taught A1 language throughout a coherent outing.
speaking_outcome: Prepare for an outing, clarify travel information, request what you need, respond to invitations and speak in four everyday encounters.

title: 1.1 What people look like
unit_outcome: Describe people and family, say what people do every day and how often, and ask about other people’s habits.
goal: Say what a person looks like (tall, short, young, old, long hair, a beard) and find the person someone describes.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 1.1 Meet the People: He is a man. becomes He is an old man. It adds no new grammar relationship: be + a description (Luis is tall.), has + a feature (A1 3.12 has: Diego has a beard.) and a/an before a description (an old man).
prerequisite: A1 1.1 boy, girl, man, woman, he, she, is; 1.5 an; 1.9 Who…?; 3.12 has.
speaking_outcome: A breathy h in has and hair (not the Spanish j), the y sound that starts young, and an old with the n joined to old, inside the complete sentence. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 1.5 Brothers and sisters
unit_outcome: Describe people and family, say what people do every day and how often, and ask about other people’s habits.
goal: Ask How many brothers and sisters do you have?, answer with I have ..., and say who is older or younger (This is my older sister. Luis has a younger brother.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 1.5 Brothers, Sisters and Adults: brothers and sisters become a question. The one new grammar relationship is the question frame How many + family word + do you have?, built from A1's How many ...? (How many apples are there?) and Do you ...? (Do you work?), answered with A1's I have. Older and younger grow A1+ 1.1's old and young into family words, with A1 1.5's an before older (an older sister). Has returns with names (Ana has two sisters.).
prerequisite: A1 1.5 brother, sister, an; A1 Have and Has (I have, he/she has); A1 How Many? (How many apples are there?); A1 Do you ...? questions (Do you work?); A1 numbers; A1+ 1.1 old, young and the cast.
speaking_outcome: Ask How many brothers and sisters do you have? as one smooth question, and say older and younger clearly, with the -er ending. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 1.6 Always, usually, sometimes, never

speaking_outcome: Place the frequency word before the verb in one smooth sentence (My father sometimes runs in the park.), with a clear -s on the verb. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 1.7 How often do you study?
unit_outcome: Describe people and family, say what people do every day and how often, and ask about other people’s habits.
goal: Ask How often do you study at night? or How often do you work at home?, answer with always, usually, sometimes or never, and report the answer (Diego usually studies at night.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 1.7 Family Actions: studying and working become habits. The one new grammar relationship is the question How often + do you + verb?, built from A1 4.8's Do you study? and answered with A1+ 1.6's frequency words before the verb (I usually study at night.). The report uses A1+ 1.2's he/she -s, where study takes the -ies spelling (studies) and work the plain -s (works).
prerequisite: A1 1.7 studying, working; A1 4.8 Do you work? Do you study?; A1 4.10 at night; A1 4.1 at home; A1 3.9 Luis the driver; A1+ 1.2 he/she -s; A1+ 1.6 always, usually, sometimes, never.
speaking_outcome: Ask How often do you ...? as one smooth question, and say studies with a clear /iz/ ending. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 1.8 What they don't do
unit_outcome: Describe people and family, say what people do every day and how often, and ask about other people’s habits.
goal: Say what you and other people don't do as a habit, with don't and doesn't (I don't cook dinner. / Diego doesn't cook dinner.), next to what they do (Ana cooks dinner.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 1.8 What They Are Not Doing: A1 says what people are not doing right now (He is not cooking.); A1+ 1.8 says what they don't do as a habit. The one new grammar relationship is don't/doesn't + the base verb: A1's I do not becomes I don't, and he/she takes doesn't, which takes the -s off the verb (Diego doesn't cook dinner.). Listen sets it against A1's is not ...-ing (Diego is not cooking dinner.).
prerequisite: A1 1.7-1.8 cooking and not; A1 4.8 and 5.5 I do not; A1 5.7 dinner; A1 2.1 restaurant; A1 4.10 in the evening; A1 7.6 watch TV; A1+ 1.2 he/she -s (cooks, eats).
speaking_outcome: Say don't and doesn't clearly, with the final t light but present, and keep the verb without -s after doesn't (doesn't cook). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 1.9 Does your family...?
unit_outcome: Describe people and family, say what people do every day and how often, and ask about other people’s habits.
goal: Ask about someone's family with does and answer with a short answer (Does your grandmother drink tea? Yes, she does.), and ask where and who with does (Where does your aunt live? Who does your cousin live with?).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 1.9 Who Is He? Who Are They?: A1 asks who family members are (Who is he? He is the father.); A1+ 1.9 asks what they do and where they live, with does. The one new grammar relationship is the question with does + the base verb, and its short answer: Does your grandmother drink tea? Yes, she does. / No, he doesn't. Where does and Who does put a question word before it (Where does your aunt live? Who does your cousin live with?). After does the verb loses its -s, as after 1.8's doesn't.
prerequisite: A1 1.9 Who; A1 4.3 Where; A1 4.8 Do you...? and Yes, I do.; A1 5.3 drink and tea; A1 4.8 run; A1+ 1.4 aunt, uncle, cousin, lives in, with; A1+ 1.6 the grandparents' tea and coffee and the parents running in the park; A1+ 1.8 doesn't.
speaking_outcome: Ask with does and a falling-rising question tone, keep the verb without -s after does (Does she drink...?), and answer with a short answer that keeps the person (Yes, she does. / No, he doesn't.). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 1.11 With him, with her, with them
unit_outcome: Describe people and family, say what people do every day and how often, and ask about other people’s habits.

grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 1.11 Friends and People: A1 names a husband and wife, their son and daughter and a friend (The husband and the wife are talking.); A1+ 1.11 says who they do things with. The one new grammar relationship is the object pronoun after with: him, her and them replace the person (She cooks dinner with her husband. / She cooks dinner with him.), next to the subject pronouns he, she and they. Her is both the possessive (her friend) and the object (with her).
prerequisite: A1 1.11 husband, wife, son, daughter, friend; A1 1.4 children; A1 1.6 mother, father; A1 3.10 his and her; A1 7.6 play football; A1+ 1.2 reads and the he/she -s (cooks, plays); A1+ 1.4 with; A1+ 1.9 Who does ... with?
speaking_outcome: Say him, her and them clearly at the end of the sentence, linked to with (with him, with her, with them); the th of them is soft. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 2.1 Where people go
unit_title: Places, things and how we describe them
unit_outcome: Say where people go and how they get there, talk about the things people have, point things out and compare them, put things in order, and ask about favorites.
goal: Say where people go with go to and goes to (I go to the gym. / Luis goes to the gym.), with three new places: gym, pool and office.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 2.1 Places Around Me: A1 names places (It is a park.) and says what people are doing in them (The girl is running in the park.); A1+ 2.1 says where people go. The one new grammar relationship is go to + place with he/she goes, the -es spelling of go, taught against the I-form (I go to the gym. / Luis goes to the gym.) and heard against A1's is going (Luis is going to the gym.). New places: gym, pool, office.
prerequisite: A1 2.1 places (park) and It is a/an; A1 4.6 go to school; A1 6.3 I am going to; A1 6.11 goes; A1+ 1.2-1.3 the he/she -s; A1+ 1.9 Where does…?; A1+ 1.3 Ana swims and Sofia runs in the park.
speaking_outcome: Say goes with a long o and a final z sound (/ɡoʊz/), different from go; keep to the in go to the gym short. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 2.2 How do you go there?
unit_title: Places, things and how we describe them
unit_outcome: Say where people go and how they get there, talk about the things people have, point things out and compare them, put things in order, and ask about favorites.
goal: Ask and say how people go to a place (How do you go to the pool? I go by bike. / How does Luis go to the gym? He goes by car.), with A1's bus, car and bike and walk.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 2.2 Streets and Transportation: A1 names the street, the bridge, the bus, the car and the bike (It is a bus.); A1+ 2.2 asks how people go somewhere. The one new grammar relationship is the question How + do/does + go to …?, built from A1 4.8's Do you…? and A1+ 1.9's Does…?, answered with A1 6.2's by bus / by bike and walk (How do you go to the pool? I go by bike. / How does Luis go to the gym? He goes by car.). The people and places are 2.1's.
prerequisite: A1 2.2 bus, car, bike; A1 6.2 by and walk; A1 4.8 Do you…?; A1+ 1.9 Does…? and Where does…?; A1+ 1.7 How often…?; A1+ 2.1 go to / goes to, gym, pool, office.
speaking_outcome: Ask How do you go…? and How does Luis go…? with falling intonation, the do/does short and weak; answer with by linked to the vehicle (by bike). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 2.3 Things I have
unit_title: Places, things and how we describe them
unit_outcome: Say where people go and how they get there, talk about the things people have, point things out and compare them, put things in order, and ask about favorites.

grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 2.3 Common Objects: A1 names a book, a pen, a phone, a bag, a chair and a table (It is a pen.); A1+ 2.3 names four more everyday things and who has them. It adds no new grammar relationship: A1's have/has and A1+ 1.5's Do you have…?, with 1.9's short answers (Luis has a watch. / Do you have a camera? Yes, I do. / Does Ana have headphones? title: 2.4 What's this?
unit_title: Places, things and how we describe them
unit_outcome: Say where people go and how they get there, talk about the things people have, point things out and compare them, put things in order, and ask about favorites.
goal: Ask and answer What's this? with the short forms What's, It's and isn't (What's this? It's a wallet. / It isn't a phone. It's a camera.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 2.4 What Is It?: A1 asks and answers with full forms (What is it? It is a book.); A1+ 2.4 uses the short forms people say. The one new grammar relationship is the contraction of is in What's and It's, and of is not in isn't, taught against the full forms (It is a watch. / It's a watch.) and joined to A1 2.2's negative contrast (It isn't a phone. It's a camera.). The things are A1 2.3's and A1+ 2.3's.
prerequisite: A1 2.2 It is a…, not a…; A1 2.3 book, pen, phone, bag; A1 2.4 What is it?; A1 2.5 this; A1 4.2 Is it…?; A1+ 2.3 watch, wallet, camera.
speaking_outcome: Say It's as one syllable with a clear final ts, What's with a final ts, and isn't as IZ-nt with no vowel between z and n. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 2.5 This one, but that one
unit_title: Places, things and how we describe them
unit_outcome: Say where people go and how they get there, talk about the things people have, point things out and compare them, put things in order, and ask about favorites.
goal: Contrast a near thing and a far one with but (This bag is red, but that bag is blue.) and say this one and that one instead of repeating the thing (This one is red, but that one is blue.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 2.5 This and That: A1 says This is a phone. for a near thing and That is a phone. for a far one; A1+ 2.5 sets the two against each other in one sentence. The one new grammar relationship is but joining two taught clauses (This bag is red, but that bag is blue.), with this one and that one standing for the thing (A1 2.10's Which one? The red one.): This one is red, but that one is blue. Each scene has two photos from the same camera behind the speaker: in the first the speaker looks down at the near thing and touches it (this), in the second the speaker faces the far thing and points down at it (that). A but sentence plays as two turns, so the picture switches on but. Two scenes are also photographed with the colors swapped, so a picture card tells this from that, not the color alone.
prerequisite: A1 2.5 this and that; A1 2.8 colors; A1 2.10 Which one? The red one.; A1 3.12 This car is mine. (this + noun); A1 2.3 bag, chair; A1 2.2 bike; A1+ 1.5 Do you have…?
speaking_outcome: Say but short and weak (/bət/) with a small pause before it; stress the two colors (This one is RED, but that one is BLUE). Say this with a short i and that with an open a. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 2.8 My favorite color

title: 2.11 Taller than Sofia
unit_title: Places, things and how we describe them
unit_outcome: Say where people go and how they get there, talk about the things people have, point things out and compare them, put things in order, and ask about favorites.
goal: Compare two people or two things with -er than (Luis is taller than Sofia. / The bus is bigger than the car. / I am older than my brother.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 2.11 Big and Small: A1 says It is a big dog. / It is a small dog. about one thing at a time; A1+ 2.11 compares two in one photo with the -er form and than (The brown dog is bigger than the white dog.). big doubles its g (bigger). It brings back A1+ 1.1's tall, short, old and young and 1.5's older and younger, now with than (My brother is older than me.). Two people or two things share each photo: Sofia beside Luis (1.1), Luis with his older and his younger brother (1.5), a bus beside a car, a big brown dog beside a small white dog, and a grandfather beside a boy on a bench.
prerequisite: A1 2.11 big, small; A1+ 1.1 tall, short, old, young; A1+ 1.5 older, younger, my brother; A1 2.2 bus, car; A1 1.10 dog; A1 brown, white; A1+ 2.10 the brown one; A1 2.12 or.
speaking_outcome: Say than with a soft th and a weak vowel (thən), linked to the comparative (TALLer than). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 2.15 ¡Nos vemos en el parque!
unit_title: Places, things and how we describe them
unit_outcome: Say where people go and how they get there, talk about the things people have, point things out and compare them, put things in order, and ask about favorites.
goal: Spend a day in the park with Ana's friends: find people by how they arrive, what they have, light and dark colors and -er than, find who breaks each park rule with Don't, find the truth in an isn't clue, and answer Ana's friends aloud about how she comes, her favorite color, where she lives and her rabbit's name.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 2.15 Encuentro en el parque: A1 closes Unit 2 by meeting in the park; A1+ 2.15 closes A1+ Unit 2 with a day in the same kind of park and no new language. The learner finds people by how they arrive (2.1-2.2), what they have (2.3), light or dark colors (2.13) and -er than (2.11), finds who breaks each park rule with Don't (2.12, bringing back 1.3's swim), finds the camera from an isn't clue (2.4), and answers How do you go …?, What's your favorite color?, Where do you live? and What is its name? aloud for Ana (2.2, 2.8, 2.7, 1.10).
speaking_outcome: Answer four friends' questions aloud for Ana: how she comes to the park, her favorite color, which floor she lives on and the name of her rabbit.

title: 3.1 Nice to meet you
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Introduce a friend (This is my friend Luis.) and answer an introduction (Nice to meet you. / Nice to meet you, too.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.1 Greetings and Names: A1 greets people and asks and gives a name (Hello. What is your name? My name is Ana.); A1+ 3.1 introduces one person to another. It adds no new grammar relationship: This is + my friend + a name presents a person (A1 2.5's This is for a thing, A1 1.11's friend), and the fixed replies Nice to meet you. and Nice to meet you, too. answer it. Sofia and Luis introduce each other to a newcomer in a café, and Ana and Diego meet him there.
prerequisite: A1 3.1 hello, goodbye, good morning and What is your name? My name is …; A1 2.5 This is …; A1 1.11 friend; A1 4.10 night, A1 4.11 see and A1 4.12 tomorrow; A1+ 2.4 What's; A1+ 2.1 goes to the gym/pool/office/park.
speaking_outcome: Say Nice to meet you as one phrase, meet and you joined (MEET-choo is fine), and too with a long u; stress friend and the name in This is my friend Luis. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 3.2 I'm, you're, we're
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Use the short forms I'm, you're and we're (I'm at the gym. / You're tall. / We're in the park.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.2 I, You, and We: A1 says I am, you are and we are; A1+ 3.2 uses the short forms people say. The one new grammar relationship is the contraction of am and are after I, you and we (I'm, you're, we're), taught against the full forms (I am at the gym. / I'm at the gym.). Speaker perspective stays explicit: a person alone says I'm, two people together say we're, and you're is said to the other person in the photo (Sofia and Luis back to back: You're tall. / I'm short.).
prerequisite: A1 3.2 I am, you are, we are; A1 4.3 in; A1 4.10 at; A1 1.11 friends; A1+ 1.1 tall and short; A1+ 2.1 the gym, the pool, the office and the park, and go to.
speaking_outcome: Say I'm as one syllable ending in m, you're like your, and we're like weer; never add a vowel between the pronoun and the short form. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 3.3 He's, she's, they're
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Say what people are doing with the short forms he's, she's and they're (He's drinking coffee. / They're running.), and ask What's she doing?
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.3 Am, Is, and Are: A1 asks What is she doing? and answers She is reading. with the full forms; A1+ 3.3 uses the short forms. The one new grammar relationship is the contraction of is and are after he, she and they with -ing (He's drinking coffee. / They're running.), taught against the full forms, with A1+ 2.4's What's in the question (What's she doing?). Listen sets it against A1+ 1.2's habit (He drinks coffee.). The short form he's is is, never a possessive.
prerequisite: A1 3.3 What is she doing? She is …-ing; A1 1.2 the -ing actions; A1 7.6 watch TV and ride a bike; A1 4.12 now; A1+ 1.2 drinks, reads; A1+ 2.4 What's; A1+ 3.2 I'm, you're, we're.
speaking_outcome: Say he's and she's with a final z sound (heez, sheez) and they're like there; keep the -ing clear. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 3.4 No, I'm not.
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Answer yes/no questions with the negative short forms (No, I'm not. / No, she isn't. / No, they aren't.) and say what is true instead (They aren't swimming. They're running.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.4 Yes and No: A1 answers Is he …? / Are you …? with Yes, he is. / No, she is not.; A1+ 3.4 answers with the negative short forms. The one new grammar relationship is the contraction of am not and are not (I'm not, aren't), next to A1+ 2.4's isn't, in short answers (No, I'm not. / No, they aren't.) and in a denial followed by what is true (They aren't swimming. They're running.). A short answer keeps the person of the question.
prerequisite: A1 3.4 yes/no questions with be; A1+ 2.4 isn't; A1+ 3.2 I'm, you're, we're; A1+ 3.3 he's, she's, they're; A1+ 1.1 short; A1+ 2.1 the gym, the office and the pool.
speaking_outcome: Say aren't as one syllable, AHRNT, with the final t; say I'm not with the m and n joined. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 3.5 Three years older
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Say how much older or younger someone is (She's three years older than him. / He's three years younger than her.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.5 Ages 11-15: A1 asks How old are you? and answers with a number of years old; A1+ 3.5 compares two ages. The one new grammar relationship is a number of years before A1+ 2.11's comparative (She's three years older than him. / He's three years younger than her.), taught against the comparative alone (She's older than him.). Each photo shows a sister and a brother, each behind a birthday cake with number candles, so the difference can be counted. The pronoun after than is A1+ 1.11's him or her.
prerequisite: A1 3.5 How old …? and eleven to fifteen; A1 2.6 two to four; A1+ 1.5 older and younger; A1+ 1.11 him and her; A1+ 2.11 older than and younger than; A1+ 3.3 he's and she's.
speaking_outcome: Say years with a clear y and a final z sound; keep older than and younger than as one group, with than unstressed. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 3.6 Both the same age
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Say that two people are twins, are the same age, or are both sixteen (They're both sixteen.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.6 Ages 16-20: A1 asks How old is she? and answers with one age; A1+ 3.6 says what two ages have in common. It adds no new grammar relationship: both goes between they're and the age (They're both sixteen.), the same age follows they're as a description (They're the same age.), and twins is a noun after they're. Two pairs of twins and two other pairs sit behind birthday cakes with number candles from A1 3.6's range, so the ages can be read; twins and the same age are told apart in text, because a picture cannot show who is a twin. 3.4's aren't and 3.5's years older come back (They aren't the same age. She's two years older than him.).
prerequisite: A1 3.6 sixteen to twenty and How old …?; A1+ 1.5 older; A1+ 3.3 they're; A1+ 3.4 aren't; A1+ 3.5 years older than.
speaking_outcome: Say both with a long o and a soft th at the end; say the same age as one group. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 3.7 What language do you speak?
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Ask and say which languages people speak (What language do you speak? I speak Spanish and English.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.7 Where Are You From?: A1 asks where people are from (Where are you from? I am from Mexico.); A1+ 3.7 asks what language they speak. It adds no new grammar relationship: What + language opens A1 4.8's do you question (What language do you speak?), and speak takes A1+ 1.2's -s (Diego speaks Spanish.). Spanish, the A1 nationality, is also the language. A1 3.7-3.8's country photos, with their flags, show where people speak Spanish or English; the cast's languages follow their A1 countries (Ana Mexican, Luis American, Sofia Canadian, Diego Spanish) and are always said, never guessed from a picture. The 3.1 newcomer asks Ana and Diego.

title: 3.8 A Canadian nurse
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Put a nationality before a noun, with a or an and never with -s (Sofia is a Canadian nurse. / Luis is an American driver. / They're two Spanish men.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.8 Canada and Spain: A1 says a nationality after be (I am Canadian.); A1+ 3.8 puts the nationality before a noun (a Canadian nurse). The one new grammar relationship is that word order, with an before American, and an adjective that never takes -s when its noun does (two Spanish men, never Spanishes). The cast's nationalities are A1's (Ana Mexican, Sofia Canadian, Luis American, Diego Spanish); the new work photos show Ana teaching, Sofia nursing and Luis driving a bus, and 1.5's photo of Diego and his brother in Spain. Picture banks change the job or the people; nationality is told apart in Listen.
prerequisite: A1 3.7-3.8 nationalities; A1 3.9 teacher, nurse, driver; A1 2.6 two; A1+ 1.5 brothers; A1+ 2.9 men and women; A1+ 3.2 I'm, we're; A1+ 3.3 they're.
speaking_outcome: Say an American as one group (a-nAmerican); stress the noun after the nationality. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 3.9 What do you do?
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Ask about someone's work with What do you do? / What does she do? and answer with a job and where people work (She's a nurse. She works in a hospital.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.9 Professions: A1 asks What is your job? and answers I am a teacher.; A1+ 3.9 asks the way people usually do. The one new grammar relationship is What + do/does + subject + do? (What do you do? / What does Ana do?), answered with a job (She's a teacher.) or with works in + a place (She works in a hospital.). Ana is a teacher in a school, Sofia a nurse in a hospital, Luis drives a bus and Diego works in an office (A1+ 2.1).
prerequisite: A1 3.9 jobs and What is your job?; A1 2.1 school and hospital; A1 4.8 do; A1+ 1.7 works; A1+ 1.9 Does…?; A1+ 2.1 the office; A1+ 3.3 he's and she's.
speaking_outcome: In What do you do? the second do is stressed; in What does she do? keep does short (duz). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 3.12 Whose bag is this?
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Ask whose things are with Whose…? and answer with his, hers or theirs (Whose camera is this? It's hers.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 3.12 Have, Has, Mine, Yours, and Ours: A1 answers with mine, yours and ours; A1+ 3.12 asks Whose…? and answers about other people. The one new grammar relationship is Whose + noun + be + this/that/these (Whose camera is this?), answered with his, hers or theirs standing alone (It's hers. / They're theirs.). His keeps one form; hers and theirs take an s that her and their do not. 3.11's bags come back with hers after than (His bag is bigger than hers.), 2.10's which ones with the owner (Which ones are his? The black ones.), and 2.5's this one and that one with mine (Is this one yours? No, that one is mine.).

title: 3.15 Review: new people, new homes
unit_title: Meeting people and talking about them
unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Review every A1+ Unit 3 step with new people: introductions, short forms of be, short answers, ages, both, languages and nationalities, jobs, hair, 's, whose and hers, addresses with at, and want to be, with no new language.

unit_outcome: Introduce people and answer introductions, use the short forms of be, answer yes/no questions in short, compare ages, talk about languages, nationalities and jobs, describe people, say whose things are, give an address and say what you want to be.
goal: Help Ana run her building's international dinner: find the neighbors by job, by what they are doing, by their hair and by whose things they hold, find what each child wants to be and each country's food, and answer Ana's friends aloud about a guest's job, a guest's languages, Diego's brother and Sofia's bag.

The learner finds the neighbors by job with a nationality before it (3.8), by what they are doing (3.3), by her or his hair (3.10) and by whose things they hold (3.11-3.12), finds what each child wants to be (3.14) and each country's food from an isn't clue (3.4, 3.8), and answers What does she do?, What language does he speak?, Diego's introduction of his brother and Is this your bag? aloud for Ana (3.9, 3.7, 3.1, 3.4 and 3.11).

unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Say where people are in a house with upstairs and downstairs, and ask Where's…? (Where's the boy? He's upstairs.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.1 Rooms at Home: A1 says which room a family member is in; A1+ 4.1 says which floor of the house they are on. The new items are upstairs and downstairs after be (She's upstairs.), asked with the short form Where's…? (Where's the boy? He's upstairs.) and answered with 3.4's short answers (Is he upstairs? No, he isn't. He's downstairs.). Every photo shows the same staircase from the downstairs hallway, with the person on the upstairs landing or on the hallway floor at its foot, so where they are is plain to see. 2.8's What's your favorite …? comes back with A1's rooms (What's your favorite room? My favorite room is the living room.).
prerequisite: A1 4.1 rooms; A1+ 2.4 short forms; A1+ 2.8 What's your favorite …?; A1+ 3.4 short answers.
speaking_outcome: Stress the first part: UP-stairs, DOWN-stairs; say Where's as one syllable (wairz). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.2 Please turn off the TV
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Ask someone to turn a lamp, a TV or a computer on or off, and say whether it is on or off (Please turn off the TV. / The lamp is on.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.2 Furniture and Home Objects: A1 names a lamp, a computer and other home objects; A1+ 4.2 switches them. The new items are turn on and turn off in a request with please (Please turn off the TV.), 2.12's command form, and on and off after be for the state (The lamp is on. / Is the computer on? No, it's off.). Each thing is photographed twice from the same camera, on and off, with its person's hand on the switch, the remote or the key: Ana's floor lamp, Luis's TV and Diego's laptop. A request is shown with the thing still in the state it asks to change, and request banks change only the thing, never on and off, so the picture never has to decide between them; on and off are set against each other only in sentences about the state, which the picture shows. Learn and Listen play a request and its result as two turns, and the picture switches on the second turn.
prerequisite: A1 4.2 lamp and computer; A1+ 1.8 Luis watches TV; A1+ 2.12 please + a command; A1+ 2.4 it's and isn't.
speaking_outcome: Link turn on (tur-NON) and turn off (tur-NOFF); keep the f of off clear. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.6 He gets dressed and then eats breakfast
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
lesson_title: He gets dressed and then eats breakfast
sub_lesson_title: He gets dressed and then eats breakfast
goal: Tell a schoolboy's morning in order with and then, ask What does he do first? / What does he do after that?, and say how he goes to school (He gets dressed and then eats breakfast.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.6 Getting ready for school: A1 tells the morning in order with I (First, I wake up. Then, I wash my face.); A1+ 4.6 tells it about the boy with 4.5's he form. The new items are and then joining two actions of one person in one sentence, the second without he (He gets dressed and then eats breakfast.), and the question What does he do first? / What does he do after that?, which asks for the next action, not a job as in 3.9. A1 4.6's own photos are reused: each one-action photo answers a question, and each two-panel photo shows two actions left to right, so it carries an and then sentence; its reversed version, which A1 approved for the same purpose, is a wrong picture only where the reversed order is a real morning (breakfast before getting dressed, teeth before breakfast). 2.2's How does … go…? comes back (How does he go to school? He walks.), with Ana, who teaches in a school (3.9), answering How do you go to school? I go by bike.
prerequisite: A1 4.6 first, then, after that, finally; A1+ 4.5 the he form of the routine; A1+ 2.2 How do you / How does.
speaking_outcome: Join and then to the next action without a stop (and-THEN-he-eats); keep does short (duz). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.7 She cleaned the table yesterday
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Say what someone did yesterday at home with -ed (She cleaned the table yesterday. / They washed the clothes yesterday.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.7 Helping at home: A1 says what people do at home (I clean the table. / They wash their clothes.); A1+ 4.7 says what they did yesterday. The one new grammar relationship is the past with -ed (cleaned, washed, opened) and yesterday, under the user's 2026-11-13 decision to teach the past with regular -ed verbs and did only. The past has no he/she -s, so she cleaned and they cleaned are the same. A past cannot be photographed: each photo shows what its person does, and Listen sets the past against the present (She cleaned the table yesterday. / She cleans the table.). A1 4.7's photos of the schoolboy's mother and the boy are reused; the door photos are A1's two-panel changes (shut, then open), and the mother also washes in the photo of them both, so a She or He washed line never meets that photo as a wrong picture.
prerequisite: A1 4.7 open, close, clean, wash clothes; A1+ 1.2 he/she -s; A1 4.1 rooms.
speaking_outcome: End cleaned and opened with a soft d (CLEEND, OH-pund) and washed with a t (WOSHT); no extra syllable. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.8 Did you clean the kitchen?
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Ask about the past with Did you…? / Did she…? and answer Yes, I did. / No, I didn't. (Did you cook breakfast? Yes, I did.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.8 Do you…? Questions and replies: A1 asks Do you…? about habits; A1+ 4.8 asks about the past with Did, the past form of do (Did you clean the kitchen? Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.), and Did she…? after A1+ 1.9's Does she…?. After did the verb is the base form, so A1 4.8's own study and work come back as they are (Did you study yesterday? / Did you work yesterday?), under the user's 2026-11-13 decision. A1 4.8's photos of Ana and Luis at a café show Ana's answer with a thumb up or down; photos of Ana cooking, studying and at her desk show what she did; A1 4.7's photos show the mother and the boy. Listen sets Did against Do and Does, and short-answer banks set did against do.
prerequisite: A1 4.8 Do you…? Yes, I do. No, I do not.; A1+ 1.9 Does she…?; A1+ 4.7 the past with -ed.
speaking_outcome: Say did with a short i (DID) and didn't as one beat (DID-nt). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.9 Luis worked on Saturday
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Say what people did and did not do on a day of the week (Luis worked on Saturday. / He didn't work on Sunday.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.9 Days of the Week: A1 names the days; A1+ 4.9 says what people did on them. The new items are the past with on + a day (Luis worked on Saturday.), with the three -ed sounds heard in worked and watched (t) and painted (an extra syllable), and didn't + the base verb for what did not happen (He didn't work on Sunday.), the past form of 1.8's doesn't. A day cannot be photographed: each photo shows what its person does, and Listen sets the days against each other and the past against the present and the negative. A didn't line is never set against a photo that shows the activity, and a No answer uses A1 4.8's photo of Ana's thumb down. Luis works (A1+ 1.1's workday photo) and watches TV (1.8), Ana works, Diego works in his office (2.1) and paints (3.14).
prerequisite: A1 4.9 the days; A1+ 1.8 doesn't; A1+ 4.7 -ed; A1+ 4.8 Did…?.
speaking_outcome: worked and watched end in t (WURKT, WOCHT); painted has two syllables (PAIN-tid); didn't is one beat. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.10 I start work at half past eight
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
lesson_title: I start work at half past eight
sub_lesson_title: I start work at half past eight
goal: Ask and say when people start and finish work, with half past and o'clock (What time do you start work? I start work at half past eight.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.10 What Time Is It?: A1 reads whole hours; A1+ 4.10 adds half past (half past eight) and asks about the workday with What time do you…? (What time do you start work? I start work at half past nine.). It is the only Unit 4 lesson with clock times, after the user's 2026-10-31 note that A1+ drilled clock time too much; the times hang on start work and finish work. The stated time is shown by the shared teaching clock, never by a photograph: A1+ 1.1's reviewed workday photos of Ana and Luis show no clock. Picture banks change only the person, never the time, and keep each person's start and finish (and leave and arrive) photos apart because they are close scenes; Listen sets half past against o'clock.
prerequisite: A1 4.10 What time is it? / o'clock; A1+ 1.2 he/she -s; A1 6.12 What time does … leave?
speaking_outcome: Say half past as one group (HAF-past) before the hour; start and finish keep their final sounds. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.11 Ana uses it
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Use it and them after a verb instead of repeating the thing (Ana gives it to her friend. / She makes them.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.11 Everyday Verbs: A1 says what people make, use, find and give; A1+ 4.11 replaces the thing with it or them after the verb (Ana uses the computer. / Ana uses it.), after A1+ 1.11's him, her and them after with; with give, it goes before to and the person (Ana gives it to her friend.). It or them is decided by how many things the photo shows: one computer, book, phone or cat; several eggs, shoes, apples or cups. A1 4.11's photos of Ana and of a family giving a book to their daughter, and A1+ 2.10's photos of Ana and Diego holding the apples and cups they chose, are reused; two new photos show Sofia holding red shoes and Ana frying eggs, so them is clearly several things.
prerequisite: A1 4.11 make, use, find, give; A1+ 1.11 him, her, them after with; A1+ 2.10 the chosen groups.
speaking_outcome: Link the verb and it (USE-zit, GIVE-zit); them is short (thum). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.12 She swims twice a week
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Say how often people do things with once a week, twice a week and every weekend (How often does Ana swim? She swims twice a week.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.12 Tomorrow and the Week: A1 names the days of a week, the weekend, the months and the year on a calendar; A1+ 4.12 counts in them how often people do things, answering 1.7's How often…? The new items are once a week, twice a week and every weekend at the end of the sentence (Diego runs once a week.), after 1.6's frequency words before the verb (Diego sometimes paints.). How often cannot be photographed: each photo shows who does what (A1+ 1.3's swimming and running, 1.8's cooking and TV, 3.14's painting), a picture bank changes only the activity or the person, and Listen sets the frequencies against each other and against 4.9's past with a day.
prerequisite: A1 4.12 week, weekend; A1+ 1.6 always, usually, sometimes, never; A1+ 1.7 How often…?; A1+ 1.3 swims, runs.
speaking_outcome: Say once (WUNS) and twice (TWAIS) with a clear s and link a week (uh-WEEK); every weekend stresses WEEK. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.13 When is your birthday?
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Ask when a birthday is and say a date with a month and an ordinal number (When is your birthday? It's on March fifth.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.13 Months: January to June: A1 names the months and says My birthday is in July.; A1+ 4.13 asks When is your birthday? and gives the day with on + a month + an ordinal number (It's on March fifth.), bringing back 2.6–2.7's second, fourth, fifth and tenth and 3.11's Luis's. The cast's birthdays are fixed from here on: Ana March fifth, Luis June second, Sofia October tenth, Diego August fourth. A date cannot be photographed: each photo shows one cast member alone at their own birthday cake (A1 4.14's photo of Ana and three new Flash photos), a picture bank changes only whose birthday it is, and Listen sets the dates against each other.
prerequisite: A1 4.13-4.14 months and birthday; A1+ 2.6-2.7 second to tenth; A1+ 3.11 's; A1+ 3.12 Whose.
speaking_outcome: Say the date as month + ordinal (MARCH FIFTH); fifth ends in th after f, and When is links (WEN-iz). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.15 Are there any keys on the floor?
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
lesson_title: Are there any keys on the floor?
sub_lesson_title: Are there any keys on the floor?
goal: Say there are some things somewhere at home, ask Are there any…? and say there aren't any (Are there any keys on the floor? No, there aren't any.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 4.15 More at Home: A1 names the floor, the stairs, the garden and a key; A1+ 4.15 says what there is in those places, adding some and any to 4.4's there is, there are and Are there…?: some in a positive sentence (There are some shoes on the stairs.), any in a question and after aren't (Are there any keys on the floor? No, there aren't any.), with How many … are there? A1 4.15's own photos of an empty floor, empty stairs and the garden are the places without the things; three new Flash photos add keys, shoes and chairs to them, and apples on a table and books on a sofa have an edit of the same place without them. An any sentence is never set against a photo of another place, where it would also be true.
prerequisite: A1 4.4 and 4.15 there is, there are, floor, stairs, garden, key; A1 5.4 some; A1+ 4.4 Is there…? / Are there…? and How many.
speaking_outcome: Link there are (THEH-rar) and say some and any unstressed before the noun (sum SHOES, enee KEYS). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 4.17 La visita de la familia
unit_title: Life at home, every day and yesterday
unit_outcome: Say where people and things are at home, talk about the lights and machines, ask what there is, describe someone's morning in order, say what you did yesterday and on which day, ask and tell the time, say how often you do things and give dates.
goal: Help Ana with her family's visit: find the things in her living room, where each family member stands, who hides where in a game of hide-and-seek and which lamp is on or off, and answer Ana's friends aloud about the kitchen, her grandmother's birthday, how often the boy plays football, a painting and the apples.

(4.7-4.8, 4.11), When is your grandmother's birthday? (4.13), How often does he play football? (4.12), Did you paint this last year? (4.9, 4.14) and Are there any apples? (4.15). 4.10's clock times stay in 4.10.
speaking_outcome: Answer four friends aloud for Ana: that she cleaned the kitchen yesterday, the date of her grandmother's birthday, how often the boy plays football, who painted the painting and where the apples are.

title: 5.2 A little rice, a lot of pasta

sub_lesson_title: A little rice, a lot of pasta
goal: Say how much food there is with a lot of and a little (There's a lot of pasta. / There's a little rice.), and tell a little from 5.1's a few.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.2 Food: A1 names food (bread, rice, chicken, fish) and says who eats or cooks it; A1+ 5.2 says how much of a food there is. The photos show a big heap against one small spoonful of the same food.
prerequisite: A1+ 5.1 a lot of and a few; A1 5.2 rice, A1 5.13 cheese; A1+ 2.4 contractions (there's); A1+ 1.2 eats.
speaking_outcome: Say a little as one phrase (a-LIT-tle, a very short); keep there's short; do not require native-like speed.

title: 5.3 Would you like some tea?
unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
goal: Offer a drink with Would you like some …? and accept or refuse it (Yes, please. / No, thank you.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.3 Drinks: A1 names drinks and says who drinks them, and A1 5.10 answers an offer with Yes, please. / No, thank you.; A1+ 5.3 makes the offer: Would you like some + a drink? It is one new frame, learnt as a whole (would is not taken apart), with A1+ 4.15's some; hot chocolate is the one new drink. In each photo a host holds out a drink and the guest takes it or holds up a hand, so the photo shows the reply. The asker's voice always differs from the answerer's (Ana and Sofia share one voice, as do Luis and Diego). I'd like waits for 5.9.
prerequisite: A1 5.3 tea, coffee, juice, water; A1 5.10 Yes, please. / No, thank you.; A1+ 4.15 some; A1 5.5 I like.
speaking_outcome: Say Would you like as one phrase (WOOD-ja-LIKE is fine) with rising intonation at the end of the offer; do not require native-like speed.

title: 5.4 How much milk is there?

goal: Ask how much of a food or drink there is (How much milk is there?) and answer with a lot of, a little or isn't much (There isn't much milk.), next to How many for things you count.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.4 How Many? and Some: A1 asks How many … are there? and counts; A1+ 5.4 asks about a food or drink you do not count, with How much + the food + is there? prerequisite: A1 5.4 How many … are there?; A1+ 5.1 a lot of, a few; A1+ 5.2 a little; A1+ 4.4 Is there…?, there isn't; A1 5.3 milk, juice.
speaking_outcome: Say How much milk with the stress on much and milk; join isn't much (IS-nt-MUCH); do not require native-like speed.

speaking_outcome: Join want to (WAN-tuh) and need to (NEED-tuh) with a short to; do not require native-like speed.

title: 5.7 Before dinner, after dinner
unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
goal: Say what you do before or after a meal (Ana washes her hands before dinner. / I drink coffee after breakfast.) and ask What do you do after dinner?
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.7 Meals: A1 says what I eat for breakfast, lunch and dinner and at what time; A1+ 5.7 places an action before or after a meal (Ana washes her hands before dinner. / Luis cleans the table after dinner.), with A1+ 1.2's he/she -s and the I-form. This is the before/after topic that left A1+ Unit 1 for A1 5.7 (2026-11-09); four of its 2026-10-31 dinner photos come back. A photo can show a meal waiting (a full plate) or finished (an empty plate), so only those photos set before against after; otherwise before and after are told apart by ear. A1+ 4.7's past comes back with cooked (Luis cooked dinner yesterday.). No clock times.
prerequisite: A1 5.7 breakfast, lunch, dinner, for lunch; A1+ 1.2 he/she -s; A1 4.7 clean; A1+ 4.5 washes; A1+ 4.7 -ed and yesterday; A1+ 1.7 What do you do …? frames.
speaking_outcome: Stress the meal after before and after (before DINner, after BREAKfast); do not require native-like speed.

title: 5.8 How much are the apples?
unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
goal: Ask the price of more than one thing (How much are the apples?) and understand the answer (They're three dollars.), next to How much is …? It's ….
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.8 Prices: A1 asks How much is …? about one named thing and the seller answers It is … dollars; A1+ 5.8 asks about more than one thing with How much are the … ? and answers with They're … dollars., next to How much is the cake? It's ten dollars. In each photo one thing (a bag of apples, a basket of oranges, a bunch of bananas, a box of strawberries, a cake) stands behind its own price card. Here How much asks a price, after 5.4's How much milk is there? asked an amount. Prices stay at ten dollars or less; bigger numbers come in 5.12.
prerequisite: A1 5.8 How much is …?, dollars; A1+ 3.3 they're; A1+ 2.4 it's; A1 numbers one to ten; A1 5.1 fruit.
speaking_outcome: Join How much are (how-MUCH-ar) and stress the price in They're THREE dollars; do not require native-like speed.

title: 5.9 I'd like a sandwich, please
unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
goal: Order politely at a café with I'd like …, please. and understand the question What would you like?
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.9 Ordering Politely 1: At a Café: A1 orders with Can I have …, please? and hands things over with Here is your …; A1+ 5.9 orders with I'd like …, please. and understands the waiter's What would you like?, after 5.3's Would you like …? offer. I'd like is learnt as a whole (the short form of would is not taken apart). Each cast member stands at the café counter with what they ordered; the waiter is never pictured, so a narrator in a voice other than the customer's asks. Listen sets I'd like against A1's Can I have …?
prerequisite: A1 5.9 Can I have …, please?; A1+ 5.3 Would you like …?; A1 5.13 sandwich; A1 5.14 cup, of, cake; A1+ 4.15 some.
speaking_outcome: Say I'd like as one word-group (IDE-like), with the d short; do not require native-like speed.

title: 5.10 Anything else?
unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
goal: Understand the seller's Anything else? and answer it: ask for one more thing (Yes, I'd like some bananas, please.) or finish (No, that's all, thank you.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.10 Ordering Politely 2: At the Market and Shops: A1 asks for things with quantities and accepts or declines an offer; A1+ 5.10 keeps a purchase going or ends it. The seller asks Anything else?, and the customer asks for one more thing with 5.9's I'd like … or finishes with That's all, thank you. Both new items are learnt as fixed phrases. At the market stall Luis points at bananas and Diego at apples, Ana waves with a full bag; at the café (5.9) Ana and Sofia finish their order. The seller is never pictured; a narrator in a voice other than the customer's asks.
prerequisite: A1+ 5.9 I'd like …, What would you like?; A1+ 5.3 Would you like …?; A1+ 5.8 How much are …?; A1 5.10 Yes, please. / No, thank you.; A1+ 3.1 too.
speaking_outcome: Say Anything else? with rising intonation (EN-ee-thing ELSE?) and That's all as one group (that-SALL); do not require native-like speed.

grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.11 Buying Things: A1 says a thing is cheap or expensive; A1+ 5.11 compares two prices with A1+ 2.11's than: a short adjective takes -er (cheaper), and a long one takes more (more expensive), the one new relationship. Each photo shows two things of one kind side by side with their price cards, so every comparison is true of one photo only; a bank never offers the converse sentence that is also true (The black bag is more expensive than the red bag.). Which … is cheaper? is answered with A1+ 2.10's one. 5.6's want to comes back.
prerequisite: A1 5.11 cheap, expensive, buy; A1+ 2.11 -er than; A1+ 2.10 Which …? The red one.; A1 5.12 the tens; A1+ 5.6 want to.
speaking_outcome: Say more expensive as one group with the stress on PEN (more ex-PEN-sive) and cheaper with CHEAP; do not require native-like speed.

title: 5.12 Forty-five dollars
unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
goal: Say and understand prices and ages from twenty-one to ninety-nine (The shoes are forty-five dollars. / She's seventy-four.), and tell forty-five from fifty-four.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.12 Numbers 30 to 100: A1 says the tens from thirty to one hundred; A1+ 5.12 joins a ten and a unit with a hyphen (forty-five = forty + five), the numbers kept out of A1+ since Unit 2 (house numbers stayed at twenty or round tens). Four numbers are taught as items and the others are practised with the same rule. Banks set a number against the one with its digits swapped (forty-five / fifty-four). Each photo shows one thing behind its price card, or a grandparent behind a cake with two number candles; 5.8's How much is/are …? asks and 5.11's cheaper than returns.
prerequisite: A1 5.12 thirty to ninety; A1 numbers one to nine; A1+ 5.8 How much are …? They're …; A1+ 3.5 How old …?; A1+ 5.11 cheaper than.
speaking_outcome: Stress the ten and keep the unit clear (FOR-ty FIVE); keep the -ty of forty short so it is not heard as fourteen; do not require native-like speed.

title: 5.14 Can you pass the salt, please?
unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
lesson_title: Can you pass the salt, please?
sub_lesson_title: Can you pass the salt, please?
goal: Ask someone at the table to pass something (Can you pass the salt, please? Here you are.) and ask for or offer a piece of cake.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.14 At the Table: A1 names things at the table (salt, sugar, cup, glass, bottle, plate, cake) and says what a cup or a glass holds (a cup of tea); A1+ 5.14 asks for something at the table with Can you pass the …, please?, a request answered by A1 5.9's Here you are., and adds a piece of for part of a cake, next to 5.3's Would you like …? and 5.9's I'd like …. Can is a request here, not ability. In each photo one cast member hands a thing across the table to the one who asks; the asker's voice always differs from the giver's.
prerequisite: A1 5.14 salt, sugar, cake, of; A1 5.9 Here you are.; A1 5.2-5.3 bread, water; A1+ 5.3 Would you like …?; A1+ 5.9 I'd like ….
speaking_outcome: Join Can you pass as one group (kn-you-PASS) and say a piece of with of short (a-PEE-suv); do not require native-like speed.

unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
lesson_title: Review: at the market and the table

goal: Review every A1+ Unit 5 step with new people: a lot of, a few and a little, Would you like …?, How much and How many, So do I, want to and need to, before and after meals, How much are …?, I'd like, Anything else?, cheaper and more expensive, numbers to ninety-nine, What's in it? and Can you pass …?, with no new language.

title: 5.16 Un sábado de compras
unit_outcome: Say how much and how many, offer and order food and drinks politely, agree about likes, say what you want and need to do, talk about meals, prices and what is in your food, compare prices, use numbers to ninety-nine and ask for things at the table.
goal: Spend Saturday with Ana and Luis at the market, a shop and a café: find shoppers by how much fruit they have, things by their price, the cheaper and the more expensive bag and watch, what café customers want, how much food is on each plate and what is in each dish, and answer aloud for Ana: agree, refuse an offer, finish shopping and say a price.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 5.16 Un día en el mercado y el café: A1 closes Unit 5 with market purchases and a café order; A1+ 5.16 closes A1+ Unit 5 with Ana and Luis's Saturday at the market, a shop and a café, with no new language. The learner finds shoppers by a lot of / a few (5.1), things by their price (5.12), the cheaper and the more expensive bag and watch (5.11), what café customers want to do (5.6), how much rice or pasta is on each plate (5.1-5.2) and what is in each dish (5.13), then answers aloud for Ana with So do I. (5.5), No, thank you. to an offer (5.3), That's all (5.10) and They're three dollars. (5.8). Every mission photo is new and used only here.
speaking_outcome: Answer four times aloud for Ana: agree with Luis, refuse his offer politely, finish shopping and tell Diego the price of the apples.

title: 6.1 Is there a bakery near here?
unit_outcome: Ask whether a place is near, say how people go to work and why they go somewhere, find a platform or gate, pack for a trip, find places on a street, follow and ask for directions, ask permission, buy tickets, understand delays and check in at a hotel.
lesson_title: Is there a bakery near here?
sub_lesson_title: Is there a bakery near here?
goal: Name four more places in town and ask whether one is near (Is there a bakery near here? Yes, there's one on Park Street.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 6.1 Places Around Town: A1 names useful places; A1+ 6.1 adds four more and asks whether one is near. The new items are bakery, bookstore, police station and gas station, the phrase near here after 4.4's Is there…? (Is there a bakery near here?) and the answer there's one + where it is (Yes, there's one on Park Street.), with 4.4's No, there isn't. Each new place is a photo whose window, car or pump shows what it is without any sign. A Yes answer is shown with that place; a No answer only with A1's shopping street, which has no gas station and no police station.
prerequisite: A1 6.1 places; A1 3.13 streets; A1+ 4.4 Is there…? and short answers.
speaking_outcome: Stress the place: BAKE-ry, BOOK-store, po-LICE sta-tion, GAS sta-tion; link there's one (therz-WUN). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 6.10 Could you tell me where the bank is?
unit_outcome: Ask whether a place is near, say how people go to work and why they go somewhere, find a platform or gate, pack for a trip, find places on a street, follow and ask for directions, ask permission, buy tickets, understand delays and check in at a hotel.
lesson_title: Could you tell me where the bank is?
sub_lesson_title: Could you tell me where the bank is?
goal: Ask a stranger politely where a place is and whether it is far (Could you tell me where the bank is? Is it far? No, it's near here.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 6.10 Can You Help Me Get There?: A1 asks Can you help me? and How do I get to…?; A1+ 6.10 asks a stranger more politely and checks the distance. The new items are Could you tell me where the … is? (the place before is, as in a statement), Is it far? and its answers No, it's near here. / Yes, it's far. Take a taxi. (far as an adjective after A1 6.6's far from). A1 6's Ana asks the man on the street; 6.6-6.7's corner, park and turn photos show the answers: the man showing Ana a short route on a street map, or a nearby street, for near here, and A1 6's town map, with the airport far across town, for far. The answer No, it's near here. brings back 6.1's near here.
prerequisite: A1 6.6 far from; A1 6.10 How do I get to…?; A1+ 6.1 places, 6.6 on the corner and opposite, 6.7 Turn left at ….
speaking_outcome: Say Could you as COOD-juh; keep where the bank is in statement order. Link is it far (iz-it-FAR). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 6.11 A round-trip ticket, please
unit_outcome: Ask whether a place is near, say how people go to work and why they go somewhere, find a platform or gate, pack for a trip, find places on a street, follow and ask for directions, ask permission, buy tickets, understand delays and check in at a hotel.
goal: Buy a one-way or a round-trip ticket and ask its price (A round-trip ticket, please. How much is a one-way ticket?).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 6.11 Which Bus Do I Need?: A1 asks Can I have a ticket, please?; A1+ 6.11 chooses the kind of ticket. The new items are one-way and round-trip before ticket (A round-trip ticket, please.), the clerk's question One-way or round-trip? with its short answers, and A1 5's How much is …? for the fare with a price up to twenty (It's ten dollars.). The two ticket photos show the kind of ticket with an arrow: one arrow for one way, an arrow at both ends for there and back. A photo of a purchase cannot show the kind of ticket, so Sofia's and Diego's ticket-window photos are only heard with a dialogue, never offered as a choice between one-way and round-trip.
prerequisite: A1 6.11 Can I have a ticket, please?; A1 5 How much is …? and dollars; A1 6 airport and station.
speaking_outcome: Say ONE-way and ROUND-trip with the stress on the first part. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 6.12 The train is late
unit_outcome: Ask whether a place is near, say how people go to work and why they go somewhere, find a platform or gate, pack for a trip, find places on a street, follow and ask for directions, ask permission, buy tickets, understand delays and check in at a hotel.

speaking_outcome: Say on TIME as two words with the stress on time; EAR-ly. Do not require native-like speed.

title: 6.13 I have a reservation
unit_outcome: Ask whether a place is near, say how people go to work and why they go somewhere, find a platform or gate, pack for a trip, find places on a street, follow and ask for directions, ask permission, buy tickets, understand delays and check in at a hotel.
goal: Check in at a hotel: say you have a reservation, take your key and ask what floor your room is on (I have a reservation. Here's your key. It's on the fifth floor.).

Four photos follow Ana through one hotel: at the front desk with her passport, taking her key, stepping out of the elevator and smiling in her room. title: 7.1 What's wrong? My head hurts
unit_title: Everyday needs, plans and free time
unit_outcome: Say what hurts and why someone feels a certain way, describe what people are wearing and the weather as it happens, tell someone to put on or take off clothes, talk about what people like doing, invite and answer, ask someone to repeat or explain, talk about being sick, the months and seasons, compare with the biggest and the tallest, and say what people and animals can do and are good at.
goal: Say what hurts with hurts and hurt (My head hurts. / My feet hurt.) and ask What's wrong?.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 7.1 My Body: A1 names the body (This is my head. I have two feet.); A1+ 7.1 says what hurts. The one new grammar relationship is a body part + hurts or hurt: one thing takes hurts (My head hurts.) and two take hurt (My feet hurt. / My legs hurt. / My eyes hurt.), with my, his and her before the body part; the question is What's wrong?. Four new photos show the cast in pain: Sofia's head, Luis's feet after a walk, Diego's legs after a run and Ana's eyes at a bright screen, and A1 7.2's tired and sad come back in front of the reason (I'm tired and my legs hurt.).
prerequisite: A1 7.1 the body; A1 7.2 How are you? tired and sad; A1 3.10 his and her; A1+ 3.4 short forms of be.
speaking_outcome: Say hurts with a clear s (HURTS) after head, and hurt with no s after feet, legs and eyes; say What's wrong? as two words (WHATS-RONG). Do not require native-like speed.

title: 7.2 Why is she cold? Because it's windy
unit_title: Everyday needs, plans and free time
unit_outcome: Say what hurts and why someone feels a certain way, describe what people are wearing and the weather as it happens, tell someone to put on or take off clothes, talk about what people like doing, invite and answer, ask someone to repeat or explain, talk about being sick, the months and seasons, compare with the biggest and the tallest, and say what people and animals can do and are good at.
lesson_title: Why is she cold? Because it's windy
sub_lesson_title: Why is she cold? Because it's windy
goal: Ask why someone feels a certain way with Why …? and answer with Because … (Why is she cold? Because it's windy.).
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 7.2 How Are You?: A1 asks how someone is and answers with a feeling (How is she? She is sad.); A1+ 7.2 asks why. The one new grammar relationship is Why + be + person + feeling? answered with Because + a reason (Why is she cold? Because it's windy.), then joined into one sentence (She's cold because it's windy.). The reasons are things A1 and A1+ already taught: the weather (A1 7.4), being sick (A1 7.9), running (A1 Unit 1) and 7.1's hurts.
prerequisite: A1 7.2 How are you? feelings; A1 7.4 weather; A1 7.9 sick; A1+ 3.3 he's/she's + -ing; A1+ 7.1 hurts.
speaking_outcome: Say Why with a rising start and a falling end (WHY is she COLD?); say because as bi-KOZ with the stress on the second part. Do not require native-like speed.

unit_outcome: Say what hurts and why someone feels a certain way, describe what people are wearing and the weather as it happens, tell someone to put on or take off clothes, talk about what people like doing, invite and answer, ask someone to repeat or explain, talk about being sick, the months and seasons, compare with the biggest and the tallest, and say what people and animals can do and are good at.
goal: Say what people like doing with like/likes + -ing (She likes dancing.), ask Does she like…? and What do you like doing?.
grammar_function: A follow-up of A1 7.6 What I Like to Do: A1 says I like to + verb (I like to dance.); A1+ 7.6 says what other people like doing. The one new grammar relationship is like/likes + the -ing form of the activity (She likes dancing. / I like painting.), with he/she + likes (the -s of A1+ 1.2), the question Does she like …? with the short answers Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't. prerequisite: A1 7.6 I like to + the eight activities; A1+ 1.2 he/she + -s; A1+ 1.8 doesn't; A1+ 1.9 Does …?; A1+ 3.3 -ing.
speaking_outcome: Say likes with a clear s (LAIKS) and the -ing ending as one soft syllable (DAN-sing, PAIN-ting). Do not require native-like speed.
